Adsum inpiger. Fac nolle, comitabor gemens Malusque patiar, facere quod licuit bono. Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt (Seneca, Moral Epistle 107 , n.11 Verses attributed to Cleanthes) The Problem of the Whispering Earring (or Bob’s Smart Glasses) Scott Alexander’s Whispering Earring imagines a magical earring that tells its wearer exactly what to do in every situation. He insists: the earring is always right . By “always right,” he does not mean that it makes the best possible decisions in every situation, but that it always makes a better decision than its wearer would have done, even after careful thought. I would like to introduce a modified version of the whispering earring for us to consider, but let’s change the earring into smart glasses to make it more true to the moment. Now let’s say the smart glasses interface with a perfect AGI model, so that their wearer, we shall call him Bob, can ask the model to supply him with answers to all questions relevant to daily life. Let’s say that one day Bob does not want to deliberate or think about his actions and decides that he will rely on his smart glasses for all of his decisions and tasks.

title: Introducing the Porphyrian Tree of Virtue
description: A New Way to Study the Virtue Theory of St. Thomas Benozzo Gozzoli, “The Triumph of St. Thomas over Averroes,” 1468-1484, via Wikimedia Commons. We are very happy to announce something that’s been years in the making: an enormous project. The Thomistic Institute, along with the Four Pillars Project at the University of St. Thomas (MN), has funded a Scientia Salon on the Theory and Practice of Virtue. This group of experts took up the task of creating a Porphyrian tree of virtue, presenting the theory of St. Thomas Aquinas in all its hierarchical glory. “What, though, is a Porphyrian Tree?” your friend wonders aloud. It’s named after the 3rd-century philosopher Porphyry, a follower of Aristotle who had a penchant for pictorial representations. To make one, you start with a concept, say, substance, then provide exhaustive distinctions between types. Maybe substance is divided between material and immaterial. Then you move to that step, further subdividing the varieties. Material divides into living and non-living; living between the sensible and insensible; sensible between the rational and irrational. If you work out all the types in all the branches, you’ve got yourself a whole tree of distinctions, which is enough to make any philosopher’s heart pitter-patter. That’s what we did with Aquinas’s views of virtue. It is really something to behold. You should go behold it . But before you zip away, let me say a bit about what’s over there. View Virtue Tree The Scholars of the Scientia Salon Thomas’s thought is so broad in scope, yet also so detailed in its sophistication, that it can sometimes be hard to navigate.

title: Why is Public Discourse so Hard?
description: Close to a decade ago, a dear friend of mine talked me into joining an important committee at the school our kids then attended. She said she foresaw difficult discussions coming our way, and she wanted more people on the committee who were able to keep their heads in heated discussions and share careful, calm reasoning. Let’s call her Huldah , after the Old Testament prophetess who saw what was to come. I’m a Philosophy professor who studies virtue in the Christian intellectual tradition. That means that my job, as philosopher, has me disagreeing cordially all day long, and the content of my research has me thinking through how to do that well. So, she didn’t misfire when she asked me to join the committee. And yet, I was hardly prepared for the crowded, acrid meetings that came to pass. Nicolas Andrre Monsiaux, “The Debate of Socrates and Aspasia,” via Wikimedia Commons , 1801. While there were reasonable, understanding people on both sides of the debate, they were the minority. One woman used her thumb and pointer finger to mimic shooting herself in the head when she disliked points being made. Others emphatically rolled their eyes, sneered, chortled, or groaned. Folks would use their allotted time to snootily express platitudes, as if a tautology would prove a substantive policy point, or to aggressively shout assertions, as if disdain or force were the main methods of discussion. And, of course, the worst actors on either side agitated the more moderate members of the other. When it came to respectful and charitable discussion, to flip the phrase, the whole was worse than its parts. The whole process was ugly, and it tore apart a community that otherwise had been healthy and vibrant. The culture of the place changed drastically.
